name: Algorithmic Colour Grading
title: Algorithmic Colour Grading
answer: Algorithmic colour grading refers to the use of software models to adjust hue, saturation, luminance, contrast, and colour balance across a still image or video sequence. In visual arts and generative illustration, it sits between raw image generation and final presentation, often applied to harmonise disparate elements or to impose a consistent palette. Unlike manual grading in a colour suite, algorithmic grading can learn from reference images or style targets and apply those relationships to new work. It is used in film, photography, illustration, and generative art pipelines.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work typically runs on standard GPU workstations or cloud rendering services, using frameworks such as PyTorch or TensorFlow for learned models and OpenCV or DaVinci Resolve for deterministic transforms. Many generative illustration tools embed grading as a post-processing step within the same inference pipeline that produces the image. For video, the process may require per-frame processing with temporal smoothing, which increases memory and compute demands. Some lightweight models run on consumer laptops, while high-resolution or real-time grading leans on dedicated graphics hardware.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The most common approach is to train a convolutional network or a lightweight colour transform model on pairs of ungraded and graded images, or on a target style reference. The model learns a mapping in a perceptual colour space, often CIELAB or a log-encoded RGB space, rather than raw pixel values. Deterministic methods may use histogram matching, white balance correction, or 3D lookup tables generated from a reference palette. In generative illustration, the grading step can be conditioned on a text prompt or a style embedding, so the same base image can be graded toward different moods without regenerating the underlying content.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on provenance and the distinction between a graded image and a newly generated one. If a grading model is trained on a cinematographer's or colourist's work, the resulting style may reproduce protected expression, and the output can raise questions of derivative use. Provenance metadata should record whether colour was altered algorithmically, especially when the image is used in journalism or evidence. Some jurisdictions treat automated colour changes as a mechanical transformation with no new authorship, while others may recognise a human's selection of reference and parameters as creative input. The site's tracking of active intellectual property lawsuits reflects how unsettled these questions remain, though colour grading itself is rarely the sole subject of a dispute.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward real-time, temporally stable grading for video and interactive media, with models that preserve skin tones and memory colours while shifting overall mood. Generative illustration tools are likely to expose grading as a separate, editable layer rather than a baked-in step, allowing artists to adjust the grade after generation. We can expect more use of reference-based grading where a single still or a short clip defines the palette for an entire sequence. As models become smaller and faster, algorithmic grading will move further into mobile capture and live streaming, with the main challenge being consistency across frames and devices.
